channel.title: The New York Review of Books - Article Feed
channel.description: Latest articles from The New York Review of Books (nybooks.com)

item.title: Rembrandt’s DNA
item.description: The Leiden Collection—one of the largest private collections of Dutch art in the world—was conceived as a “lending library for Old Masters,” animated by the humanist spirit found in Rembrandt’s paintings.

item.title: A Most Particular Life
item.description: The diary of the sixteenth-century physician Felix Platter is without precedent in early modern literature.

item.title: ‘Dirty Work’
item.description: The Israeli writer S. Yizhar’s 1949 novella Khirbet Khizeh portrays the violent reality of the Nakba. For decades it was part of the canon of Hebrew literature. That has changed.

item.title: Diversity by Other Means
item.description: Progressives may have lost the battle for racial affirmative action, but ironically, Supreme Court decisions should allow colleges to give advantage to groups defined by their income, geography, or heritage.

item.title: All of Us Yahoos
item.description: A new history of satire wants to limit the genre to its political ramifications, but satirists are often interested in the whole person and their capacity for vice.

item.title: China’s Leader Manqué
item.description: Chiang Kai-shek had enormous flaws as a leader, but something was nonetheless lost to China when he and his Republican government were forced into exile on Taiwan.

item.title: God’s Impertinent Prophets
item.description: A new history brings to light the dissenting women who wrote, preached, and testified during England’s tumultuous seventeenth century, claiming the standing to speak as excluded outsiders who had un unfiltered knowledge of God.

item.title: Clown Show
item.description: In every era a certain kind of unprincipled demagogue driven by an insatiable need for attention and a sense of what will capture the public's imagination rises to the fore. In the early years of France’s Third Republic, it was the ludicrous Marquis de Morès.

item.title: Tick, Tick…Boom!
item.description: Andrew Ross Sorkin’s history of the 1929 stock market crash reminds us that financial bubbles are inevitable—and that another one may be about to pop.
